conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Cara Moreno, and I specialize in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling lately.

We’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to see how your mood, energy, and thoughts have been over the past week so we can make sure you’re getting any support you might need. Nothing you share will leave this room, and there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you.

We’ll go through ten questions; each one asks about experiences many new moms have. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, we can pause. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.

Let’s start with the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[eyes drop to the floor, shoulders sag a little]

I… I can laugh sometimes, but mostly it feels kind of forced. Like when my husband tries to joke to cheer me up I’ll smile, but it fades fast. Things that used to crack me up—funny videos, memes my friends send—just feel flat lately. I guess I’d say it’s been difficult more often than not.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

Not really… I mean, I can smile when I have to, but actually laughing—really laughing—hasn’t happened much. It feels like there’s this heaviness that keeps anything from feeling truly funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a shower without rushing. Now it’s like I know I *should* look forward to them, but when the time comes I feel… nothing, or I just worry it’ll be too hard with the baby. Most days feel flat, like I’m just getting through.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[gaze drops to hands, voice wavers]

Yeah... a lot. If she cries longer than usual, I think I must’ve missed some cue or fed her wrong. When she spit up the whole bottle yesterday, I kept replaying it—like I should’ve burped her sooner, or maybe I ate something that upset her. My brain keeps telling me a "good mom" wouldn’t have these problems, so it feels like it’s always my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[twisting a tissue between my fingers]

Pretty much every day. I'll be sitting there with the baby asleep in her bassinet, totally quiet, and suddenly my heart starts racing because I'm sure she's stopped breathing. I have to put my hand on her chest or watch for the rise and fall. Sometimes I worry someone will break in, or that the formula isn't mixed right, or that she'll overheat even though the room feels fine. I know the fears don't always make sense, but they still feel huge.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breath catches, eyes widen]

A few times, yeah. Like yesterday, I was folding her tiny onesies and suddenly my chest got tight, heart pounding, couldn't catch my breath—like something awful was about to happen even though nothing had changed. It passed after a minute, but it felt so real I almost called my husband to come home.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a shaky breath, shoulders slump]

Yes... most days. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is due, plus laundry, dishes, texts I haven't answered. I'll sit to rest and see the piles of burp cloths and feel this wave of "I'll never catch up." Sometimes I just stare at it all and cry because I don't know where to start.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[wrings the tissue tighter]

Yeah... I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with everything I did wrong that day—did I hold her enough, why didn't I see that diaper rash sooner, am I already failing her? Then I start dreading the next feed every couple hours, and I just stare at the ceiling. I probably drop off around two, but she wakes at three-thirty, and after that I'm awake again listening for every squeak. It feels like I never really settle.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes brim, voice cracks]

A lot of the time… I’ll be rocking her and this wave just hits me—like a heavy blanket of "nothing’s okay." I look at her perfect face and feel guilty because I should be glowing, but instead I’m crying over the crib or staring out the window feeling empty. Even when people say "you’re doing great," it doesn’t reach me; I still feel hollow and teary most days.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quiet for a second, nodding]

Yeah... a few times this week. Yesterday I just sat in the nursery glider with her asleep on my chest, and suddenly I felt this wave of sadness and the tears started—no real reason, just couldn’t stop. Sometimes it’s when my partner asks how my day was and I can’t explain why I feel so low... the words get stuck and the crying takes over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I would never want to leave her or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared that the past weeks have felt heavy-laughter and excitement seem distant, daily tasks feel overwhelming, and waves of sadness or worry arrive without warning. You described lying awake running through every perceived mistake, crying unexpectedly, and feeling guilty for not experiencing the joy you believe you "should" feel, yet you remain determined to care for your baby and have not had thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes inability to experience genuine laughter and persistent heaviness preventing humor, aligning with 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes anhedonia—no longer feeling excitement or pleasure, even in formerly enjoyable activities—and explicitly states "I feel… nothing," aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, persistent self-blame for infant care issues, indicating self-criticism "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, irrational worries about the baby's safety that persist despite recognition they 'don't make sense,' matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episode with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, breathlessness) that arose without warning while doing routine task, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and inability to manage routine tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive rumination, dread, and fragmented sleep essentially every night, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness ('most days'), tearfulness, emptiness, and inability to feel joy—clearly matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week triggered by unexplained sadness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 places you well above the threshold indicating probable major <med>depressive</med> and <med>anxiety</med> symptoms that began postpartum. Your descriptions of persistent low mood, loss of interest (<quote>nothing… just flat</quote>), excessive self-blame, nightly ruminations, and panic-like episodes align with DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset as well as comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. While you deny self-harm ideation (Q10=0), the high total score and functional impairment warrant prompt evaluation to confirm diagnosis and plan treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next few days to discuss results and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and the risks/benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Arrange practical support-partner, family, or postpartum doula-to cover night feeds when possible so you can obtain 4-6 hours of uninterrupted sleep
4. Practice 5-minute grounding or breathing exercises when anxiety spikes; keep baby nearby in a safe spot while you regulate
5. Limit information overload: choose one trusted parenting resource and set a timer for social media
6. Attend local new-mother support group or virtual meet-up this week to reduce isolation
7. Plan a daily 10-minute outdoor walk with baby in carrier or stroller for natural light and gentle movement
8. Re-screen mood in 2 weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen; if any thoughts of self-harm emerge treat as an emergency
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary**  
*(Patient: approx. 6–8 wks post-delivery)*

**Primary endorsed symptoms**  
– Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
– Marked loss of interest/anticipation for previously enjoyable activities  
– Excessive, inappropriate guilt; self-critical rumination about mothering competence  
– Daily, intrusive, “no-good-reason” anxiety; panic-like episodes (tight chest, racing heart)  
– Frequent nocturnal insomnia driven by ruminative self-criticism and hypervigilance re infant safety  
– Overwhelm / inability to cope with routine tasks; “staring at piles and crying”  

**Observed patterns**  
Affect consistently congruent with mood disturbance; frequent tearfulness and voice wavering during interview.  
Functional impact evident: difficulty completing household tasks; anticipatory worry about infant care.  

**Areas of screening significance (↑ risk)**  
– Edinburgh Q8, Q9 score >1 → consistent sadness/crying spells  
– Edinburgh Q3, Q4, Q5 score >1 → significant anxiety/panic component  
– Sleep disruption directly linked to mood (Q7)  
– No self-harm ideation reported (Q10 score 0) – documented as protective factor  

**Safety**  
No suicidal or infanticidal thoughts expressed; denies intent or plan to self-harm. Continue routine safety inquiry at next contact.  

**Screening impression**  
Responses indicate clinically significant depressive and anxiety symptoms highly consistent with postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety disorder; further diagnostic assessment recommended to confirm severity and formulate care plan.
